rv.q: Big, brassy, unapologetically profane and over the top — it's no wonder Bette Midler signed on as a producer.
Inartful here, crass there, this rollicking crowdpleaser in sequins nonetheless packs enough heart to leave the masses enthralled.
Despite a tendency to hit the jokes too hard, the show floats along on a lovable bus of beaded lights, tropical interior and bushels of shredded Mylar.
Priscilla is a well-above-average drag show with the pink afterimage of a plot, and three superbly sincere leads who fleetingly convince us we’re seeing an actual musical with a real emotional arc.
Some people -- many people, likely -- won't be able to get enough of 'Priscilla,' Others may be put off by its relentless naughtiness
Priscilla Queen of the Desert has colorful artifice to spare—those costumes!—but nearly nothing about it rings true.
But while it is performed with gleaming verve and infusions of bawdy humor
The show is simultaneously too much and not enough: too much noise and glitter, not enough heart and specificity.
Priscilla is so sound, so right, and after seeing it, I can't imagine it any other way.
The weakest element is Swenson, who seems a bit ill at ease as Tick/Mitzi.

As a result, the show is as thin as a bulimic egret's feather, but when it clicks, it's as infectious as a rabid koala because the zingers keep coming along with the costumes, and by the end, they're all dressed like animals and dancing to a disco medley!
"Priscilla" will do anything to try to entertain - even stooping to dragging audience members on stage for a dance number - and it succeeds often enough to be appealing.

While the show will likely prove to be a crowd-pleaser, it can be difficult to tell whether all of those offering a standing ovation at the curtain call actually enjoyed what they saw — or are simply surrendering out of sheer exhaustion.
The first tipoff to the desired ambiance at 'Priscilla Queen of the Desert' is severe-faced Broadway ushers sporting huge purple boas.
Call me a party pooper, but that was enough to make this supposed frolic a drag.
You really want to have fun, but it is so aggressively campy that it soon becomes irritating and too much to stomach.

A wildly flashy musical version of a 1994 cult film, "Priscilla, Queen of the Desert" sashayed into the Palace on Sunday, all fun, fantastic frocks and fabulousness - but not really all that much heart.
